newsitem.title: USA: Ball in Sinn Fein court, UK's Blair says.
newsitem.headline: Ball in Sinn Fein court, UK's Blair says.

text.p: Britain will not wait for ever for the IRA to declare the unconditional ceasefire needed to gain a seat for its political wing, Sinn Fein, at Northern Ireland's peace talks, Prime Minister Tony Blair said on Saturday.

Blair told reporters at the annual summit of the Group of Seven industrial nations that he was determined to push toward a lasting settlement of the British-ruled province's political problems -- with or without Sinn Fein.
"The people of Northern Ireland have got the right to expect the government to push this process forward with or without Sinn Fein -- so the ball is in their court," he said.

Blair hopes renewed support from U.S. President Bill Clinton, who expressed his outrage after the IRA murdered two policemen in Northern Ireland last Monday, will be instrumental in putting the peace process back on track.
"The important thing is that even here in America, where Sinn Fein used to rely on some support, people are right behind the British government," Blair said.
As he spoke, Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams issued a statement in Belfast rejecting Blair's criticism of the IRA over the murders as "short-termism."
Adams, whose party and the IRA advocate a united Ireland, said the main stumbling block to Sinn Fein's entry into peace talks was "decommissioning" -- the surrender of IRA arms.
"Decommissioning has not yet been removed as an obstacle in the negotiations. This remains the biggest stumbling block," Adams said.
Northern Ireland was expected to be at the top of the agenda at the first of two bilateral meetings that Clinton and Blair have scheduled on Saturday on the fringes of the Denver summit.

"What's important is that the strength of feeling here is that we've done the right thing and now it's up to them to decide whether they really want to be part of this or not, because we can't wait for ever," the British prime minister said.

Britain broke off contacts with Sinn Fein after Monday's murders and is demanding that the IRA renew in word and in deed the ceasefire that it ended in February 1996 when it launched a string of bomb attacks to further its aim of driving Britain out of Northern Ireland.
Blair sidestepped a question on whether he would ask Clinton to break off all contact with Sinn Fein.

What was important, he said, was that Clinton should know that the new Labour government had done everything it could to draw Sinn Fein in to the multi-party peace talks being chaired by former U.S. Senator George Mitchell.
"I think the change in feeling here in the United States is because people have seen the British government go that extra way to try to make sure this process is inclusive of SF.
"There's a strong recognition here, as there is back in the United Kingdom that that process can't wait upon Sinn Fein," he added.
